a: Joshua was old, far along in years
t: The second half of the book
p: The war stories are over. From here the book turns to maps, borders and town lists, and to Joshua's farewell.
b: Chapters 13–21 divide the land, chapter 22 sends the eastern tribes home, and chapters 23–24 are Joshua's last words. The opening line also starts a tension that runs through the rest of the book. 11:23 said Joshua "took the whole land," yet here God says that a great deal is still left to take, and 21:43–45 will again say every promise came true. Traditional readers take the summaries as true in principle: the power of the Canaanites was broken, but mopping up remained (Judges 1). Critical scholars see two views of the conquest set side by side, a sweeping one and a gradual one. Either way, the book itself does not hide the gap.

a: all the regions of the Philistines
p: Sea Peoples from the Aegean world who settled the southern coast early in the 1100s BC.
b: Egyptian records of Ramesses III describe his battle with the "Sea Peoples," among them the Peleset, early in the 1100s BC. Digs at Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron and Gath show a new culture arriving then, with Aegean-style pottery, hearths and diet (including pork). Amos 9:7 and Jeremiah 47:4 say they came from Caphtor, usually taken as Crete. The name Palestine comes from them through Greek. Their five cities are listed in 13:3. The word for "regions" (gelilot, "circles, districts") is related to Galilee, "the circle."

a: the Shihor, which faces Egypt
p: Shihor comes from Egyptian "pool of Horus," a branch of the Nile or a lake on the eastern edge of the Delta.
b: In Isaiah 23:3 and Jeremiah 2:18 the Shihor is clearly in Egypt and stands for the Nile. Here and in 1 Chronicles 13:5 it marks the far southwest limit of the land, so some take it as the same border as the "Wadi of Egypt" (15:4; Numbers 34:5), and others as a waterway at the edge of the Delta. Either way, the land "still left" reaches to Egypt's doorstep.

a: the five rulers of the Philistines
p: The word for these rulers, seren, is used only of the Philistines. It may be a borrowed foreign word.
b: The Hebrew Bible has no other use of seren for a ruler; it always means the lords of the five Philistine cities (Judges 16:5; 1 Samuel 5:8; 6:4). Many scholars connect it with the Greek tyrannos, "ruler," or with a word in Luwian, a language of Asia Minor. If so, the title itself points to the Philistines' Aegean roots. Each lord ruled a city, and together they acted as a council.

a: in the south
p: An older people of the coast near Gaza, pushed out by newcomers from Caphtor.
b: Deuteronomy 2:23 says, "As for the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, the Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor, wiped them out and settled in their place." A remnant may be meant here. "In the south" could also be read with the next verse ("from the south, all the land of the Canaanites"). The Hebrew allows both.

a: the land of the Gebalites
p: Gebal is the Phoenician port of Byblos, north of Beirut, a center of the papyrus trade.
b: Gebal (modern Jbeil in Lebanon) is one of the oldest towns on earth. Its craftsmen cut stone for Solomon's temple (1 Kings 5:18) and caulked the ships of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:9). Greeks called it Byblos, and because papyrus came through it, byblos came to mean "papyrus" and biblion "book." The English word Bible comes from this. The list in 13:2–6 sweeps from Philistia in the south to Lebanon and Lebo-hamath in the north (see the note on Numbers 34:8). Israel never held most of it, though David's power reached far north (2 Samuel 8).

a: I myself will drive out before the Israelites
p: God tells Joshua to hand out by lot even the land Israel does not yet hold. The promise comes before the possession.
b: Joshua is to allot it now and trust God to clear it later. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers see faith here: the map is drawn on God's word. Some point to David and Solomon, whose rule came close to these limits (1 Kings 4:21). Critical scholars read the northern and coastal claims as an ideal map of the promised land, like Numbers 34, never matched by Israel's real borders. The verse also explains why later chapters speak of nations that "remain" (23:4–13): they were left as a test (Judges 2:20–3:4).

a: had already received their inheritance
t: The deal made east of the Jordan
p: Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh asked Moses for the grazing land east of the Jordan and got it.
b: Numbers 32 tells how the two and a half tribes asked for the land of Sihon and Og, and how Moses agreed on condition that their men cross over and fight with their brothers (Numbers 32:20–32; Deuteronomy 3:12–20). Joshua held them to it (1:12–18), and in 22:1–9 he sends them home. This chapter first records what Moses gave them (13:8–33), so that the map of all twelve tribes is complete before the lots are cast west of the Jordan.

a: Aroer on the edge of the Arnon Valley
p: The Arnon (Wadi Mujib) is a canyon about 1,700 feet deep that cuts the high plain east of the Dead Sea.
b: It was Moab's northern border in Moses' day (Numbers 21:13). Aroer is Khirbet Arair, on the north rim. On the Mesha Stele, about 840 BC, King Mesha of Moab boasts, "I built Aroer, and I made the road in the Arnon." "The town in the middle of the valley" is unknown. The "high plain" (mishor, "level ground") is the tableland north of the Arnon, good for flocks.

a: one of the last of the Rephaim
p: Og is remembered as the last of an old race of giants.
b: Deuteronomy 3:11 says, "Only Og king of Bashan was left of the last of the Rephaim. Look, his bed was a bed of iron." Ugaritic texts use rpum of the honored dead, and Ashtaroth and Edrei, Og's cities, appear in an Ugaritic text as the seat of a god. So the Rephaim stood both for giants and for shades of the dead (Isaiah 26:14). See the topic page.

a: Geshur and Maacah live among Israel to this day
p: Two small Aramean kingdoms north and east of the Sea of Galilee were never driven out.
b: Geshur lay on the Golan, east of the lake. David married Maacah daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, and their son Absalom fled to his grandfather there (2 Samuel 3:3; 13:37–38). The phrase "to this day" appears again in 14:14, 15:63 and 16:10. Brevard Childs showed that it usually adds a writer's own witness to an older tradition. Traditional readers take it as a sign the book was written while these things were still true; critical readers ask which "day" is meant.

a: The offerings by fire to the LORD
p: Levi gets no land. Its inheritance is the LORD's offerings, the LORD himself, and the priesthood.
b: Joshua says it three ways: the offerings by fire are Levi's inheritance (13:14), the LORD is its inheritance (13:33), and the priesthood is its inheritance (18:7). Deuteronomy 18:1 joins the first two: "They will eat the LORD's offerings by fire, which are his inheritance." Instead of fields, the Levites lived from the gifts brought to God, and they received towns among all the tribes (chapter 21).

a: the leaders of Midian
p: The five leaders killed in the Midian war are here called princes of Sihon, perhaps his vassals.
b: Numbers 31:8 names the same five: "they put to death the five kings of Midian: Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba." Here they are linked to Sihon. The word nesikhim is rare; it may mean princes who had been installed or anointed, that is, vassal rulers under Sihon. The verse joins two of Moses' wars in one memory.

a: the diviner
p: Here Balaam gets the label qosem, "diviner," a practice Deuteronomy forbids.
b: Numbers 22–24 shows Balaam speaking God's words, and he is never called a diviner there, though Balak's men carry "fees for divination" (Numbers 22:7). Joshua uses the plain word qosem, which Deuteronomy 18:10 names among the practices banned in Israel. Numbers 31:16 blames him for the sin at Peor, and Joshua records his death among the enemy. See also 24:9–10.

a: Lo-debar
p: The Hebrew Lidbir is read as Lo-debar by many, as Debir by the KJV.
b: The consonants could name a Debir east of the Jordan (KJV), but most scholars think this is Lo-debar, a town in Gilead. There Mephibosheth lived before David sent for him (2 Samuel 9:4), and Amos mocks Israel for celebrating its capture: lo-davar sounds like "nothing at all" (Amos 6:13).

a: Havvoth-jair, the tent villages of Jair
p: The villages Jair son of Manasseh captured in Gilead or Bashan.
b: Numbers 32:41 says, "Jair son of Manasseh went and captured their tent villages, and called them Havvoth-jair." Deuteronomy 3:14 places them in Bashan, and the judge Jair later had thirty sons who ruled thirty towns by that name (Judges 10:3–4). 1 Chronicles 2:21–23 traces Jair through Hezron of Judah, a reminder that clans moved between tribes.

a: The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance
p: God's word to Aaron becomes a prayer of every faithful Israelite.
b: God told Aaron, "I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites" (Numbers 18:20). The psalms use the same land words for anyone who trusts God: "The LORD is the share I was given, and my cup. You are the one who keeps my lot safe. My boundary lines have landed in lovely places" (Psalm 16:5–6), using goral, "lot," and chevel, "measuring line" (there "boundary lines"), the words of this part of Joshua. Compare Psalm 73:26 and Lamentations 3:24.

a: by Eleazar the priest
p: Numbers 34:16–29 named who would divide the land. Here they do it.
b: The priest comes first, as in Numbers 34:17, 19:51 and 21:1. The "family heads" are the tribal leaders listed in Numbers 34:19–28. So the division west of the Jordan is shown as Moses' plan carried out, not Joshua's own scheme. Chapters 14–19 have two settings: Gilgal (14:6) for Judah and Joseph, and Shiloh (18:1) for the other seven tribes.

a: Their inheritance was given by lot
p: A lot (goral) was a marked stone or stick drawn from a jar or a fold of cloth. Israel took the result as God's choice.
b: "People throw the lot into the lap, / but every verdict it gives comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). Numbers 26:54–56 asks for both size and lot: a big tribe gets a big share, but the lot decides where. The Talmud says Eleazar, wearing the Urim and Thummim, named each tribe and region before the draw, and the lot then agreed (Bava Batra 122a). Our phrase "my lot in life" comes from this practice.

a: The descendants of Joseph were two tribes
p: Levi has no land and Joseph counts twice, so there are still twelve shares.
b: Jacob adopted Joseph's sons: "Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine as much as Reuben and Simeon are" (Genesis 48:5). That double share is the firstborn's portion, which passed from Reuben to Joseph (1 Chronicles 5:1–2). With Levi set apart for God, Ephraim and Manasseh fill out the twelve.

a: Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite
p: The Kenizzites appear among Edom's clans. Caleb's family may have joined Judah from outside.
b: Kenaz is a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:11, 15), and the Kenizzites are listed among the peoples of Canaan in Genesis 15:19. Many scholars, traditional and critical, think Caleb's clan was of Edomite or southern origin and was taken into Judah. If so, the man held up as the model of faith in this chapter is an adopted Israelite, like Rahab before him and Ruth after. Numbers 13:6 counts him as Judah's leader.
r: Genesis 15:19; Genesis 36:11; Genesis 36:15; Numbers 13:6; Numbers 32:12; 1 Chronicles 2:18–20

a: I brought him back word as I truly saw it
p: Literally "I brought back word as it was with my heart": an honest report, not one shaped by fear.
b: The heart in Hebrew is the seat of thought and will, not only feeling. Caleb means he reported what he really believed. The other spies let fear shape their words (Numbers 13:31–33), while Caleb said, "we will win against it, without a doubt" (Numbers 13:30). His heart matched his words; theirs made the people's hearts melt (14:8).

a: made the people's hearts melt
p: The same image Moses used for the spies' report forty-five years earlier.
b: Moses remembered Israel's complaint: "Our brothers have made our hearts melt" (Deuteronomy 1:28). In Joshua the image is turned around: it is the Canaanites whose hearts melt when they hear what God did (2:11; 5:1). Caleb's point is that fear, not giants, kept the first generation out.

a: I followed the LORD my God fully
p: The Hebrew idiom is "to fill after," meaning to follow without holding back. It is Caleb's signature.
b: The phrase comes three times in this chapter (14:8, 9, 14) and is used of Caleb, and Joshua, in Numbers 14:24 and 32:12: "they have followed the LORD fully." Elsewhere it appears only in the negative, of the generation that died in the wilderness (Numbers 32:11) and of Solomon, who did not follow the LORD fully as David had (1 Kings 11:6). The rabbis and the church fathers alike made Caleb a model of wholehearted faith.

a: The land your foot has walked on
p: The promise comes from Numbers 14:24 and Deuteronomy 1:36.
b: Deuteronomy 1:36 reads, "I will give him and his sons the land his feet have walked on, because he followed the LORD fully." Caleb had walked through Hebron as a spy (Numbers 13:22), so Hebron is what he asks for. The words also echo God's promise to Joshua that every place the sole of his foot stepped would be his (1:3).

a: Forty-five years have passed
p: Caleb's numbers suggest the wars of chapters 6–12 lasted about seven years.
b: Caleb was 40 at Kadesh (14:7), in the second year after the exodus. Israel then spent about 38 more years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 2:14). Forty-five years later he is 85, so about seven years have passed since the crossing of the Jordan. The rabbinic chronicle Seder Olam counts it this way: seven years of conquest and seven of dividing the land. 11:18 says, "Joshua made war a long time."

a: Perhaps the LORD will be with me
p: Caleb, a man of strong faith, says "perhaps." Readers have taken it in different ways.
b: Some hear modesty: Caleb will not presume on God, even with a promise in hand. Others hear the same bold hope as Jonathan's "Maybe the LORD will act for us" (1 Samuel 14:6) or the king of Nineveh's "Who knows?" (Jonah 3:9). Either way, Caleb asks for the hardest ground in the land, the fortress towns of the Anakim, at age 85.

a: Kiriath-arba
p: Arba means "four." The text explains it as a man's name; Jewish tradition also read "Town of Four."
b: This verse and 15:13 make Arba a great man of the Anakim. A rabbinic midrash read "Town of Four" because four couples were buried there in the cave of Machpelah: Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah (Genesis Rabbah 58:4; Rashi on Genesis 23:2). Some modern scholars think of four allied clans or quarters. Genesis 23:2 already calls Hebron by this name.

a: Then the land had rest from war
p: The same words close the war stories in 11:23. They frame Caleb's gift as part of the peace.
b: The Hebrew shaqat, "be quiet, at rest," becomes the refrain of Judges after each deliverance (Judges 3:11; 3:30; 5:31; 8:28). It is different from the verb for the "rest" God gives in 21:44 and 22:4 (nuach).

a: The lot for the tribe of the people of Judah
t: Why Judah's list is so long
p: Judah gets more space than any other tribe: a full border and about 115 towns in eleven or twelve districts.
b: Judah comes first and in detail because Judah became the kingdom that kept these records. Scholars agree that the town list (15:20–62) is grouped in districts, but not on its date. Albrecht Alt tied it to Josiah's kingdom (about 630 BC); Frank Cross and G. Ernest Wright to Jehoshaphat (about 870 BC); others to Hezekiah or to the united monarchy. Traditional readers take it as Joshua's allotment, brought up to date as towns grew. Either way the lists are real geography, and many towns can be located today.

a: from the tongue of water that points south
p: The Hebrew says "the tongue." It is the shallow south bay, cut off by a peninsula still called el-Lisan, "the tongue."
b: A broad peninsula, el-Lisan (Arabic for "the tongue"), juts into the Dead Sea from the east and divides a deep northern basin from a shallow southern one. The border starts at the southern tip. The north border likewise starts at "the tongue of the sea at the mouth of the Jordan" (15:5), and Benjamin's south border ends at "the north tongue of the Salt Sea" (18:19).

a: This will be your south border
p: The "your" gives it away: Judah's south border repeats Moses' south border for the whole land.
b: Numbers 34:3–5 runs the same line: the Salt Sea, the Scorpion Pass, Zin, Kadesh-barnea, Azmon, and "From Azmon the border will turn to the Wadi of Egypt and end at the sea" (Numbers 34:5). Joshua keeps Moses' second person. So Judah's south edge is Israel's south edge. Ezekiel 47:19 uses it again for the land restored.

a: the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben
t: A Reubenite stone west of the Jordan
p: A landmark named after a Reubenite stands on the Judah–Benjamin border, west of the Jordan.
b: Bohan means "thumb," so it may have been a thumb-shaped rock. Why a son of Reuben would be remembered here is a puzzle. Some think part of Reuben once lived west of the Jordan before settling east; others see a memorial of the eastern tribes' service in the conquest (compare 22:10). It appears again on Benjamin's border (18:17).

a: from the Valley of Achor
p: The valley where Achan was stoned (7:24–26) lies on Judah's border. The prophets turned its name into hope.
b: Achor means "trouble" (see 7:26). Hosea promises that God will make "the Valley of Achor a door of hope" (Hosea 2:15), and Isaiah 65:10 pictures it as a resting place for herds. Many place it in the Buqeia, the basin above Qumran, though this is debated.

a: Gilgal, which faces the Ascent of Adummim
p: This is not Israel's camp near Jericho. The same spot is called Geliloth in 18:17.
b: Both names come from galal, "to roll," and mean "circle(s)," perhaps stone circles. The Ascent of Adummim ("red rocks") is the climb from Jericho to Jerusalem, past red limestone. Jesus' story of the Good Samaritan is set on this road (Luke 10:30), and a later shrine there is called the Inn of the Good Samaritan.

a: En-rogel
p: A spring just south of Jerusalem where the Kidron and Hinnom valleys meet, today Bir Ayyub.
b: David's men hid there to get news during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 17:17), and Adonijah held his feast there when he tried to make himself king (1 Kings 1:9). The border runs right under the walls of the Jebusite city, as the next verse shows.

a: the Valley of Ben-hinnom
p: This valley's name became "Gehenna," the word Jesus used for hell.
b: Ge ben-Hinnom, "valley of the son of Hinnom," runs west and south of old Jerusalem. Here it is only a boundary. Later kings burned children there to Molech at a place called Topheth (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31–32), and Jeremiah renamed it the Valley of Slaughter. By Jesus' time its Aramaic name, Gehinnam, Greek geenna, meant the place of final punishment (Mark 9:43–48).

a: the south slope of the Jebusite city, that is, Jerusalem
p: The line runs just south of the city, so Jerusalem itself falls to Benjamin (18:28), not Judah.
b: The Hebrew says "the shoulder of the Jebusite." Jerusalem was already an old city: the Amarna letters of the 1300s BC include letters from its king Abdi-Heba to Pharaoh, calling it Urusalim. Placed on the seam between Judah and Benjamin, it belonged to neither until David took it and made it his capital (2 Samuel 5:6–9).

a: Baalah, that is, Kiriath-jearim
p: "Town of forests," also called Baalah and Kiriath-baal, where the ark stayed for twenty years.
b: It is usually placed at Deir el-Azar above Abu Ghosh, west of Jerusalem. It was one of the four Gibeonite towns (9:17). After the Philistines sent the ark back, it stayed here in the house of Abinadab until David brought it up to Jerusalem (1 Samuel 7:1–2; 2 Samuel 6:2, where it is called Baale-judah). The old name Baalah, "lady" or "Baal's town," was replaced by a name without the god.

a: Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai
p: Here Caleb drives them out. In 11:21–22 it is Joshua, and in Judges 1:10 the men of Judah.
b: The spies saw these three at Hebron (Numbers 13:22). Traditional readers harmonize: Joshua's campaign broke their power (11:21), Caleb finished the job at Hebron with Judah's help (Judges 1:10–20). Critical readers see several traditions credited to different heroes. Both agree that the book presents Caleb's success as the reward of his faith (14:12).

a: Debir used to be called Kiriath-sepher
p: Kiriath-sepher means "town of the scroll." Its site is debated: Tell Beit Mirsim or Khirbet Rabud.
b: W. F. Albright dug Tell Beit Mirsim in the 1920s and 30s and named it Debir. Most scholars now favor Khirbet Rabud, southwest of Hebron, which Moshe Kochavi excavated; it lies in the hill country where 15:49 places Debir and has two wells in a nearby valley, known locally as the upper and the lower, which some match with the upper and lower pools of 15:19. The Greek translators rendered the name "city of letters." 15:49 also calls it Kiriath-sannah.

a: I will give him my daughter Achsah as his wife
p: Caleb offers his daughter to the man who takes the town. Modern readers find this hard; the story itself gives Achsah a voice.
b: Saul does the same for the man who kills Goliath (1 Samuel 17:25; 18:17–27). In the ancient world marriage was arranged by fathers, and a hero for a son-in-law strengthened the clan. Many recent readers note that Achsah does not stay passive: she gets down, asks, and wins water for her land (15:18–19). Compare Judges 1:12–15, which tells the same story, and the very different end of the daughter of Jephthah (Judges 11).

a: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's brother
p: The Hebrew can mean Othniel was Caleb's brother, or that Kenaz was. Judges 3:9 says "Caleb's younger brother."
b: If Othniel is Caleb's brother, he marries his niece. If Kenaz is Caleb's brother, Othniel marries his cousin. Both were allowed. Many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, take Othniel as Caleb's younger brother, as Judges 3:9 seems to say. Othniel becomes the first judge of Israel (Judges 3:7–11), so the family of the faithful spy produces the first deliverer.
orig: עָתְנִיאֵל בֶּן־קְנַז אֲחִי כָלֵב (otni'el ben-qenaz achi khalev)

a: She got down from her donkey
p: The verb tsanach comes only here, in Judges 1:14 and in Judges 4:21. Its sense is not certain.
b: Most translators take it as "got down, slipped off," a sign of respect before a request (as Abigail does in 1 Samuel 25:23). The Greek translators seem to have guessed "she cried out." Others suggest a gesture such as clapping her hands. In Judges 4:21 the same verb is used of Jael's tent peg going down into the ground.

a: Give me a blessing
t: A blessing that is a gift
p: Berakhah, "blessing," can mean a gift. Achsah asks for something solid: water.
b: Jacob urges Esau, "Please take my blessing" (Genesis 33:11), meaning his gift of flocks. The Negev, the dry south, was poor land without water. The "pools" (gullot, "basins") were springs or pools fed by springs; some match them with two wells near Khirbet Rabud, the likely site of Debir, which local names call the upper and the lower. Achsah's bold request is granted in full.

a: twenty-nine towns in all
t: Totals that do not add up
p: The Negev list names about 36 towns but counts 29. Several district totals in Joshua differ from the names given.
b: Possible reasons: some pairs are one town ("Ain and Rimmon" is En-rimmon in Nehemiah 11:29); some names were added later from Simeon's list (19:2–7), which shares many of these towns; scribes may have copied a name twice. The totals seem to belong to an older form of the list. The differences are a reminder that the text grew and was copied, not that the writers could not count.

a: In the Shephelah
p: The "lowland," a belt of low hills between Judah's mountains and the coastal plain, fought over for centuries.
b: Its valleys were the gateways into the hill country, so Philistines, Assyrians and Babylonians all fought here. David met Goliath in the Valley of Elah between Socoh and Azekah (15:35; 1 Samuel 17:1). Lachish (15:39) was its strongest city. The Lachish Letters, written on potsherds about 588 BC, include one in which an officer says they can no longer see the signals of Azekah, exactly as Jeremiah 34:7 names Lachish and Azekah as the last cities holding out.

a: Ekron, with its towns and villages
p: Ekron, Ashdod and Gaza are listed for Judah, though 13:3 says they were not taken.
b: Judah's list claims the land to the sea, as God's grant, even where Philistines ruled. Judges 1:18 says Judah took Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, but Judges 1:19 adds that they could not drive out the people of the plain. Ekron is Tel Miqne, where in 1996 excavators found a royal inscription naming the city and its king Achish (Ikausu), from the 600s BC. "Its towns" is literally "its daughters," the small towns that depended on a city.

a: the City of Salt
t: Secacah and the City of Salt
p: Six towns in the Judean wilderness by the Dead Sea. Some link the City of Salt with the site of Qumran.
b: In the 1950s Frank Cross and J. T. Milik surveyed the Buqeia valley above Qumran and found small Iron Age forts, which they matched with Middin, Secacah and Nibshan. An Iron Age fort lies under the Qumran ruins, so some identify Qumran with the City of Salt, and others with Secacah, which also appears in the Copper Scroll found at Qumran. En-gedi, an oasis spring, is where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 24:1).
r: 1 Samuel 23:29; 1 Samuel 24:1; Song of Songs 1:14; Ezekiel 47:10

a: But the people of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites
p: Judah could not take Jerusalem. Judges 1:21 says the same of Benjamin. David finally took it.
b: Judges 1:21 is almost the same sentence, but with Benjamin instead of Judah, fitting 18:28, which gives the city to Benjamin. Judges 1:8 says Judah once attacked Jerusalem and burned it, but the Jebusites held on. David captured the fortress of Zion (2 Samuel 5:6–9). "To this day" suggests the note was written before David. Many traditional scholars take that as evidence of an early source; critical scholars agree that an early source lies behind it, even if the book was finished later.

a: The lot for the descendants of Joseph
p: Ephraim and Manasseh together held the central hills, the heart of the later northern kingdom.
b: Joseph's lot gets one outer border (16:1–3) before it is split between the two tribes. Surveys of the hill country by Israel Finkelstein and others found that the new villages of the early Iron Age (about 1200–1000 BC) were densest here, in the land of Ephraim and Manasseh. Later the northern kingdom was often called simply "Ephraim" or "the house of Joseph" (Hosea 5:3; Amos 5:6).

a: From Bethel it went out to Luz
p: Genesis 28:19 says Bethel was once called Luz. Here they seem to be two places side by side.
b: In 18:13 Luz and Bethel are the same town, as in Genesis 28:19 and Judges 1:23. Here the border runs "from Bethel to Luz." Perhaps Bethel was first the name of Jacob's holy place outside the town of Luz, and the name later spread to the town. See the topic page.

a: the Archites
p: A clan living near Ataroth. David's loyal friend Hushai was an Archite.
b: Hushai the Archite, "David's friend," stayed in Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt and wrecked Ahithophel's advice (2 Samuel 15:32–37; 17:5–14). The Japhletites in 16:3 are otherwise unknown. Both look like old clans of the region whose names stuck to their land.

a: the towns set apart for the Ephraimites inside the inheritance of the Manassites
p: Ephraim held some towns inside Manasseh's land. The borders of the two brother tribes were tangled.
b: 17:8–9 gives an example: Tappuah's land was Manasseh's, but the town was Ephraim's. Manasseh likewise held towns in Issachar and Asher (17:11). Real tribal life seldom followed straight lines. The tension between the brother tribes surfaces later in Judges 8:1–3 and 12:1–6.

a: But they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer
p: A strong Canaanite city guarding the road from the coast to Jerusalem. It stayed Canaanite until Solomon's time.
b: Gezer (Tell Gezer) appears in Egyptian records: the Amarna letters include letters from its kings, and the Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) boasts "Gezer is seized" in the same lines that first name "Israel." 1 Kings 9:16 says a pharaoh captured and burned Gezer and gave it to his daughter, Solomon's wife, and Solomon rebuilt it (1 Kings 9:15–17). The Gezer Calendar, an early Hebrew farming poem on a limestone tablet, was found there.

a: but they have been put to forced labor
t: Forced labor instead of the ban
p: Instead of destroying or driving out the Canaanites, Ephraim made them a labor force. Was that obedience or failure?
b: Mas oved is a work gang owed to a ruler, unpaid labor by turns. Deuteronomy 20:11 allows it for distant towns that surrender, but 20:16 forbids sparing the peoples of the land. The book reports it without praise (also 17:13), and Judges 1:28–35 repeats it as a pattern of half obedience. Solomon later used the same system for the remaining Canaanites (1 Kings 9:20–21). Readers concerned with the ethics of conquest note that the texts show coexistence, not extermination, as what actually happened. The Greek text lacks this clause; in its place it tells how Pharaoh later took Gezer (see the variant).

a: for he was Joseph's firstborn
p: Jacob put Ephraim ahead of Manasseh, yet Manasseh is still called the firstborn.
b: When Jacob blessed the boys, he crossed his hands and gave the greater blessing to the younger, Ephraim (Genesis 48:13–20). Joshua himself was an Ephraimite (Numbers 13:8), and Ephraim's lot is listed first (16:5). But Manasseh's birthright is not erased: it holds land on both sides of the Jordan, the largest territory of any tribe.

a: because he was a fighting man
p: Machir's clan had already taken Gilead and Bashan by force (Numbers 32:39–40).
b: "The descendants of Machir son of Manasseh went to Gilead, captured it, and drove out the Amorites who were in it" (Numbers 32:39). In the Song of Deborah, Machir stands for Manasseh as a whole (Judges 5:14). "Father of Gilead" makes Machir the ancestor of the clans of that region.

a: the descendants of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida
p: Several of these clan names, and two of Zelophehad's daughters, turn up as district names on the Samaria ostraca.
b: The Samaria ostraca, notes in ink on potsherds from the 700s BC found at the capital of the northern kingdom, record shipments of wine and oil from districts named Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem and Shemida, and also Hoglah and Noah (17:3). So the family names in this list were real place names in the hills of Manasseh. Gideon came from the clan of Abiezer (Judges 6:11).

a: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah
p: Moses had ruled that daughters could inherit. Now the five sisters hold the leaders to it.
b: In Numbers 27 the sisters asked Moses for their father's share, and God answered, "Zelophehad's daughters have spoken rightly. Yes, give them land to own as an inheritance among their father's brothers" (Numbers 27:7). Numbers 36 added that they must marry within their tribe. Here, a generation later, they come before Eleazar and Joshua and receive it. Tirzah later became an early capital of the northern kingdom, after Shechem (1 Kings 12:25; 14:17; 16:23).

a: among their father's relatives
p: The rabbis praised the five sisters as wise, learned and righteous.
b: The Talmud calls them wise, interpreters of Scripture, and righteous, and notes that they spoke at the right time (Bava Batra 119b). Here they show what Joshua's book shows of Caleb: they remind the leaders of what God promised and ask for it. Their case became the Bible's basic ruling on daughters' inheritance.

a: So ten shares fell to Manasseh
p: Five sons' clans plus the five daughters of Zelophehad make ten portions west of the Jordan.
b: Of Gilead's six clans (17:2), Hepher had no grandsons, so his share passed through Zelophehad to his five daughters. Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem and Shemida make five, and the five sisters another five: ten. The verse treats the women's shares as full portions, on equal terms with the men's clans.

a: the three of Napheth
p: A puzzling phrase. Napheth may mean "height" or a district, perhaps the region of Dor.
b: In 11:2 and 12:23 we read of "Naphoth-dor" or "Naphath-dor," the heights or district of Dor. So the phrase may mean "the third is Napheth," that is, Dor, or "three districts." No reading is certain, and translations vary widely.

a: the people of Megiddo and its towns
p: Beth-shean, Taanach and Megiddo guarded the great valley. Megiddo gave its name to Armageddon.
b: These cities sat on the main road between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Pharaoh Thutmose III won a famous battle at Megiddo in the 1400s BC. Beth-shean had an Egyptian garrison until about 1130 BC, and the Philistines hung Saul's body on its wall (1 Samuel 31:10). Solomon later fortified Megiddo (1 Kings 9:15). Revelation's "Armageddon" is probably "Mount Megiddo" (Revelation 16:16).

a: the Canaanites were set on living in that land
p: Judges 1:27–28 repeats these verses almost word for word and makes them the start of Israel's troubles.
b: "As Israel gained strength, they made the Canaanites do forced labor. But as for driving them out, they did not do it" (Judges 1:28). Judges then has God's messenger say the Canaanites will be "thorns" and snares to Israel (Judges 2:1–3), as Joshua warns in 23:13. The verb here, ho'il, means "to be willing, to make up one's mind." The Canaanites chose to stay, and Israel let them.

a: Why have you given me only one lot
p: The strongest tribe asks for more. Joshua, himself an Ephraimite, tells them to earn it.
b: Commentators enjoy the irony. Joseph, which received the richest hills, protests that it has only one share, while 16:1–17:13 described two. Joshua (from Ephraim, Numbers 13:8) does not favor his own tribe: if they are so many and so strong, let them clear the forest and face the chariots. Ephraim's touchy pride shows again in Judges 8:1 and 12:1.

a: go up into the forest. Clear land for yourselves there
p: The central hills were wooded. Archaeology shows Iron Age settlers clearing forest and building terraces.
b: The verb bera, "clear," is literally "cut down." Pollen studies and surveys show the hill country more wooded in the Bronze Age than today. The hundreds of small villages founded there around 1200–1000 BC cut terraces into the slopes, dug plastered cisterns for rain water, and planted grain, vines and olives. Joshua's answer matches what the earth shows: the hill country was won by hard work as much as by war.

a: iron chariots
p: Not chariots made of iron, but wooden chariots with iron fittings. They ruled the flat valleys, not the hills.
b: A popular picture makes them armored tanks. Chariots were light wooden frames, perhaps with iron rims, studs or fittings, and iron was still rare and costly. In the open valleys of Jezreel and Beth-shean they were deadly; in the forest hills they were useless. Judges 1:19 says Judah could not drive out the people of the plain because they had iron chariots, and Sisera had nine hundred (Judges 4:3).

a: came together at Shiloh, and there they set up the tent of meeting
p: Shiloh, in the hills of Ephraim, becomes Israel's sanctuary. The tent stood there until the days of Eli and Samuel.
b: Shiloh is Khirbet Seilun, about 20 miles north of Jerusalem. A Danish team dug there in 1926–32, and Israel Finkelstein led new excavations in 1981–84. Finkelstein found an Iron Age town and dated its destruction to around 1050 BC, which many link with the Philistine victory of 1 Samuel 4, though the dating is debated. Excavations under Scott Stripling since 2017 have made further claims about where the tabernacle stood, which other archaeologists contest. The Talmud says the tabernacle stood at Shiloh 369 years (Zevachim 118b). Jeremiah used Shiloh's ruin as a warning for Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7:12–14), and Psalm 78:60 says God "left the tabernacle of Shiloh behind."
r: Judges 18:31; Judges 21:19; 1 Samuel 1:3; 1 Samuel 4:3–11; Psalm 78:60; Jeremiah 7:12–14; Acts 7:45

a: The land had been brought under their control
p: The verb kavash, "bring under control," is the one God used in Genesis 1:28.
b: God told the first humans, "Fill the earth and bring it under control" (Genesis 1:28). Joseph Blenkinsopp and others noticed that the priestly writings in the Torah run from creation to the tabernacle, and on to this verse, where the tent is set up in a land brought under control. The setting up of the sanctuary in the land completes, in a small way, the order of creation. Numbers 32:22 and 29 used the same verb for the land.

a: How long will you hang back
p: Mitrappim means "letting your hands go limp." Seven tribes are dragging their feet.
b: The root rafah means to sink or go slack. Proverbs 18:9 uses it of the lazy worker, "brother to the one who destroys." The land is given, but it still has to be taken up. Joshua's question echoes God's own complaints, "How long will this people spurn me?" (Numbers 14:11).

a: write a description of it
p: Twenty-one men walk the land and write it up in a scroll, town by town, before the lots are cast.
b: The verb katav, "write," comes five times in 18:4–9. The book imagines a written record of the land, like the land registers kept in the ancient Near East. Josephus retells the scene, saying Joshua sent men who knew how to measure land and told them to judge its quality, so that poorer land could be given in larger pieces (Antiquities, book 5). The written description matters: the shares are drawn by lot, but from a fair division.

a: The lot came up for the tribe of the Benjaminites
p: The smallest tribe gets a narrow strip between Judah and Joseph, with some of the land's key towns.
b: Benjamin's strip held Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, Ramah, Mizpeh and Jerusalem itself (18:21–28). "Came up" pictures the lot rising out of a jar or a fold of cloth. Saul, Israel's first king, was a Benjaminite from Gibeah (18:28; 1 Samuel 9:1–2), and so was the apostle Paul (Philippians 3:5). Moses' blessing pictures God dwelling "between his shoulders" (Deuteronomy 33:12), perhaps a hint of Jerusalem on Benjamin's border.

a: the wilderness of Beth-aven
p: "House of wickedness": a town near Bethel. Hosea later used the name as an insult for Bethel itself.
b: Here and in 7:2 and 1 Samuel 13:5, Beth-aven is a real place east of Bethel. Some think the name was once Beth-on, "house of strength" or "house of On," and was respelled. Hosea plays on it: Bethel, "house of God," has become Beth-aven, "house of wickedness," because of Jeroboam's calf (Hosea 4:15; 10:5).

a: The border went out westward
p: Running from Kiriath-jearim to Nephtoah means going east, yet the Hebrew says "westward."
b: The same line in 15:9 runs the other way, from Nephtoah west to Kiriath-jearim. Here the Hebrew yammah ("seaward, westward") is hard to fit. Commentators suggest a copying slip, or take the word as "from the west side," describing where the line started. The NRSV instead corrects the text to "to Ephron," following 15:9 (see the variant). Benjamin's south border (18:15–19) follows Judah's north border (15:5–9) in reverse.

a: Jebus (that is, Jerusalem)
p: The Hebrew is "the Jebusite." Outside the Bible no source calls the city Jebus.
b: Egyptian texts and the Amarna letters always name the city Urusalim or something like it. Only Judges 19:10–11 and 1 Chronicles 11:4–5 call it Jebus. J. Maxwell Miller argued that "Jebus" was a name made from its people, the Jebusites, rather than the city's real old name. Here the list itself says "the Jebusite, that is, Jerusalem." The city sits in Benjamin's list, on its border with Judah (see 15:8, 63).

a: Gibeah and Kiriath
p: Gibeah, "the hill," was Saul's hometown. "Kiriath" may be short for Kiriath-jearim.
b: Gibeah of Benjamin is the scene of the outrage of Judges 19–20 and the home of King Saul (1 Samuel 10:26). It is usually placed at Tell el-Ful, just north of Jerusalem. "Kiriath" alone means "town." Since 18:14 calls Kiriath-jearim a town of Judah, some think a shorter Kiriath of Benjamin is meant; others read the two words together as "Gibeath-kiriath."

a: Their inheritance lay inside the inheritance of the people of Judah
p: Simeon gets no land of its own, only towns inside Judah. Jacob's last words had said Simeon would be scattered.
b: Jacob said of Simeon and Levi, "I will divide them among Jacob / and spread them thin through Israel" (Genesis 49:7). Levi was scattered as a priestly tribe; Simeon faded into Judah. Moses' blessing in Deuteronomy 33 leaves Simeon out entirely. 19:9 gives a practical reason: Judah's share was too big. 1 Chronicles 4:24–43 lists these same towns and tells of later Simeonite moves to Gedor and Seir.

a: Beersheba, Sheba, Moladah
p: The list names fourteen towns but counts thirteen (19:6). "Sheba" may be a copying echo of Beersheba.
b: 1 Chronicles 4:28 lists "Beersheba, Moladah" with no Sheba. The parallel in 15:26 has "Shema." Either a scribe wrote part of Beersheba twice, or Sheba is a misspelled Shema. Beersheba, at the edge of the desert, is linked with Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 21:31; 26:33) and marks Israel's southern limit in the phrase "from Dan to Beersheba."

a: Ziklag
p: Ziklag later became David's base when he hid from Saul among the Philistines.
b: Achish of Gath gave Ziklag to David: "This is how Ziklag came to belong to the kings of Judah, as it still does today" (1 Samuel 27:6). 1 Chronicles 4:31 notes of Simeon's list, "These were their towns until David became king." So the list seems to come from before David's reign, when Simeon still had its own towns. Hormah ("destruction") recalls the ban in Numbers 21:3.

a: Gath-hepher
p: The prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Zebulun, a few miles from Nazareth.
b: 2 Kings 14:25 calls Jonah son of Amittai "from Gath-hepher." It is usually placed at Khirbet ez-Zurra' near Mashhad, where Jewish and Muslim tradition show Jonah's tomb. When the leaders said, "Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee" (John 7:52), Jonah of Galilee was an exception, as later Christian writers pointed out.

a: Bethlehem
p: This Bethlehem lies in Galilee, about seven miles from Nazareth. A few scholars think Jesus was born here.
b: Beit Lahm in Galilee still bears the name. The judge Ibzan may have come from here (Judges 12:8–10). Matthew 2:1–6 and Luke 2:4 place Jesus' birth in Bethlehem of Judah, the city of David, and nearly all Christians and most scholars accept that, or read it as a statement of his Davidic line. A minority, such as the archaeologist Aviram Oshri, have argued for the Galilean Bethlehem because of its nearness to Nazareth. Only five towns are named here, though the verse counts twelve; the rest seem to be the border towns of 19:10–14.

a: Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem
p: Issachar held the rich eastern Jezreel Valley, with Jezreel and Shunem.
b: Jezreel became a royal city of Ahab and Jezebel, scene of Naboth's vineyard and of Jehu's revolt (1 Kings 21; 2 Kings 9). Shunem was home to Abishag (1 Kings 1:3) and to the woman who housed Elisha (2 Kings 4:8). Jacob's blessing pictured Issachar as "a strong donkey" who bent to forced labor for the sake of good land (Genesis 49:14–15). That fits a tribe in the open valley under Canaanite chariot cities.
r: Genesis 49:14–15; 1 Samuel 28:4; 1 Kings 1:3; 1 Kings 21:1; 2 Kings 4:8; Hosea 1:4–5

a: Tabor
p: The round mountain where the borders of Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali meet.
b: Barak gathered his army on Tabor before defeating Sisera (Judges 4:6–14). Psalm 89:12 pairs it with Hermon in praise. Christian tradition, at least from the fourth century, has located the transfiguration of Jesus here, though the Gospels only say "a high mountain" (Mark 9:2), and some prefer Hermon.

a: Cabul
p: Solomon later gave Hiram of Tyre twenty towns here. Hiram called them "the land of Cabul."
b: When Hiram saw the towns, he said, "What are these towns you have given me, my brother?" and they were called the land of Cabul (1 Kings 9:13), apparently a pun on "like nothing." Cabul (modern Kabul, east of Acco) shows how Asher's coastal land drifted into Phoenician hands.

a: as far as Great Sidon
p: Asher's line reaches Sidon and Tyre, cities Israel never held.
b: Judges 1:31–32 says Asher did not drive out the people of Acco, Sidon, Achzib and the rest, "so the Asherites lived among the Canaanites." Tyre's island fortress (19:29) held out against Assyria and Babylon and fell only to Alexander the Great in 332 BC. The border is God's grant, not a record of control. Deborah complained that Asher "sat by the seashore" instead of joining the war (Judges 5:17).

a: the great tree at Zaanannim
p: Heber the Kenite pitched his tent "by the great tree at Zaanannim." There Jael killed Sisera.
b: Judges 4:11 places Heber's camp at this tree near Kedesh, and Judges 4:17–22 tells how Sisera fled there after the battle. Elon is a large tree, an oak or terebinth; landmark trees were often holy places (Genesis 12:6). See also the oak at Shechem (24:26).

a: and Judah at the Jordan toward the sunrise
p: Judah lies far to the south, so "touching Judah at the Jordan" is one of the book's puzzles.
b: Several answers are offered. Rashi thought of Havvoth-jair east of the Jordan, settled by Jair, whose line went back to Hezron of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:21–22). Many modern scholars suspect a copying error and leave the word out, reading simply "the Jordan on the east." Others take "Judah" as an old name of some region by the Jordan.

a: The fortified towns
t: Naphtali and Galilee of the nations
p: Zebulun and Naphtali, the Galilee tribes, are where Matthew says Jesus' ministry began.
b: Naphtali's towns run along the Sea of Galilee: Hammath (hot springs near Tiberias), Rakkath and Chinnereth. Isaiah 9:1–2 promised that "the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali ... Galilee of the nations" would see a great light. Matthew 4:13–16 quotes it of Jesus settling in Capernaum "in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali." Hazor (19:36) was the greatest city of Canaan, which the book says Joshua burned (11:10–13). On the archaeology, see chapter 11.

a: Beth-anath
t: Canaanite gods in the place names
p: Beth-anath means "house of Anat," a Canaanite war goddess. Beth-shemesh means "house of the sun."
b: Anat was Baal's fierce sister in the Ugaritic myths. Beth-anath (and Beth-anoth in Judah, 15:59), Anathoth (21:18), Beth-shemesh ("house of the sun") and Baalah (15:9) keep the names of Canaan's gods. Israel took over the towns and often the names. Judges 1:33 says Naphtali did not drive out the people of Beth-anath and Beth-shemesh. The names are real evidence that Israel settled among an older religious world; they do not mean Israel worshiped those gods, though the prophets say many did.

a: Zorah, Eshtaol
p: Dan's first land lay in the low hills west of Jerusalem, Samson's home.
b: Samson was born in Zorah, and the Spirit first stirred him "between Zorah and Eshtaol" (Judges 13:2, 25). He was buried there (Judges 16:31). The Danite spies who later went north also set out from Zorah and Eshtaol (Judges 18:2). Timnah and Ekron (19:43) were Philistine towns in Samson's stories.

a: with the territory facing Joppa
p: Joppa (Jaffa) was the old port of the central coast. Jonah sailed from there, and Peter stayed there.
b: Cedar for the temple came by sea to Joppa (2 Chronicles 2:16; Ezra 3:7). Jonah ran from God through Joppa (Jonah 1:3). In Acts, Peter raised Tabitha at Joppa and there saw the vision that sent him to the Gentile Cornelius (Acts 9:36–43; 10:9–23). Me-jarkon, "the waters of the Yarkon," is the river that today flows through Tel Aviv.

a: But the territory of the Danites slipped out of their hands
p: Dan lost its land to the Amorites and Philistines and moved to Laish (Leshem) in the far north. Judges 18 tells the story.
b: The Hebrew is "the territory of the Danites went out from them." According to Judges 1:34, the Amorites pressed Dan into the hills, and Judges 18 tells how the tribe sent spies, found quiet Laish, burned it and renamed it Dan. Leshem is another spelling of Laish. Tel Dan has been excavated since 1966; there in 1993 a stone inscription of the 800s BC was found naming the "house of David." The Greek text of these verses is longer, with lines that seem to draw on Judges 1:34–35 (see the variant).

a: the Israelites gave Joshua son of Nun an inheritance among them
p: The two faithful spies frame the division west of the Jordan: Caleb receives first (14:6–15), Joshua last.
b: Readers since the church fathers have noticed that the leader takes his share only after everyone else. Literary critics such as L. Daniel Hawk point to the frame: the two men who trusted God at Kadesh open and close the handing out of the land. Joshua asks for a modest town in his own tribe's hills, not the best land. Like Caleb, he received it "at the LORD's command" (19:50; compare 15:13).

a: Timnath-serah
p: Judges 2:9 calls Joshua's town Timnath-heres, "portion of the sun." Here it is Timnath-serah, "extra portion."
b: The two names use the same letters, with the last ones reversed. Some think "serah" is a deliberate change, to avoid a name tied to sun worship. A Jewish tradition preserved by Rashi (on Judges 2:9) connects "heres" with the sun Joshua made stand still (10:12–13), saying an image of the sun was placed on his tomb. The site is usually identified with Khirbet Tibnah, northwest of Bethel.

a: at the entrance of the tent of meeting
t: The division finished before the LORD
p: The section began at Gilgal (14:1–6) and ends at the sanctuary in Shiloh. The land is God's gift, handed out in his presence.
b: This closing note repeats 14:1 almost word for word, with "at Shiloh, before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting" added. In Leviticus the entrance of the tent is where offerings are presented and judgments made (Leviticus 1:3; Numbers 27:2). "So they finished" echoes the finishing of the tabernacle (Exodus 40:33) and of creation (Genesis 2:2), the same verb kalah.

a: the cities of refuge I told you about through Moses
p: Exodus promised a place of refuge, Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19 set the rules, and here the cities are named.
b: Exodus 21:13 first promised, "I will set aside a place for you where he can run for refuge." Numbers 35:9–34 called for six cities, three on each side of the Jordan. Deuteronomy 19:1–13 required three in the land and roads kept open to them. Moses had already set apart the three eastern cities (Deuteronomy 4:41–43). Joshua 20 completes the system.

a: by mistake, without meaning to
p: "By mistake" is the wording of Numbers 35; "without meaning to" is the wording of Deuteronomy 19.
b: Bishgagah, "by mistake," is the priestly word for an unintended wrong (Numbers 35:11; Leviticus 4:2). Bivli da'at, literally "without knowing," is Deuteronomy's phrase: "someone who strikes his neighbor without meaning to, when he had not hated him in the past" (Deuteronomy 19:4). Joshua joins them. Many scholars see the chapter as a blend of the two law codes; the shorter Greek text (see 20:4) lacks much of the Deuteronomy wording.

a: stand at the entrance to the city gate
p: The city gate was the town's courtroom. The elders hear the refugee before letting him in.
b: Elders sat in the gate to judge cases (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1–2; Amos 5:15). The refugee is not simply safe once he arrives: he must tell his story, and the elders decide whether to take him in. Later the community holds a full trial (20:6; Numbers 35:24–25). The rabbis added that two scholars should go with the refugee to calm the avenger on the way (Mishnah Makkot 2:5).

a: until the high priest of that time has died
p: As in Numbers 35:25, the killer goes home only when the high priest dies.
b: Numbers 35:25 says, "He must stay there until the high priest dies, the one anointed with the holy oil." On how Jewish and Christian readers have explained this, see the note on that verse. Hebrews 6:18 speaks of believers as people "who have fled for refuge" to take hold of hope, using the language of these cities.

a: So they set apart Kedesh in Galilee
p: "Set apart" is vayyaqdishu, "made holy." The three western cities are spaced north, center and south.
b: Kedesh in the hills of Naphtali (Tel Kedesh, northwest of Hazor), Shechem in Ephraim, and Hebron in Judah all lie on or near the main road along the central ridge, about a day or two apart. The verb "made holy" ties the refuge to sacred space: all six cities were also Levite towns (chapter 21), and before this people fled to the altar (Exodus 21:14; 1 Kings 1:50). This is the first mention of Galilee (galil, "circle, district") in the Bible.

a: Bezer in the wilderness on the high plain
p: The eastern cities were already named by Moses in Deuteronomy 4:43.
b: Deuteronomy 4:43 names them: "Bezer in the wilderness, on the high plain, for the Reubenites; Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites; and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites." King Mesha of Moab claims on his stele, "I built Bezer, for it was in ruins," so it later passed to Moab. Ramoth-gilead became a frontier fortress fought over with Aram (1 Kings 22). Golan gave its name to the Golan Heights.

a: the cities set aside
p: The Bible never tells of anyone fleeing to a city of refuge. Scholars differ on whether the cities really served this way.
b: The phrase are hammu'adah, "appointed cities," appears only here. In the stories of the kings, those who seek safety run to the altar (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28). Traditional readers assume the system worked quietly, as good laws do; the Mishnah's tractate Makkot works out its rules in detail. Many critical scholars think the cities were an ideal that grew out of altar asylum, perhaps from the time of the kings or later. Alexander Rofé used this chapter, with its shorter Greek text, as a test case of how a law was expanded over time.

a: for the foreigner living among them
p: Like Numbers 35:15, Joshua extends the same protection to the ger, the foreigner who lives in Israel.
b: The ger had no clan of his own to defend him and no family land, so he was easily harmed. The law gives him the same refuge and the same trial as any Israelite (Numbers 35:15). Compare the repeated rule, "one law for the native and the foreigner" (Exodus 12:49; Leviticus 24:22).

a: with their pasturelands for our livestock
p: The migrash is the open land around a town, used for grazing, not farmland.
b: Numbers 35:4–5 set its size. Leviticus 25:34 adds that "the pastureland around their cities must not be sold, because it is their holding for all time." The Levites did not own whole towns: they had homes in them and the right to the common land outside the walls. The Levites appeal to Moses' command (Numbers 35:1–8), just as Caleb and Zelophehad's daughters did.

a: The descendants of Aaron the priest
p: All thirteen priestly towns lie in Judah, Simeon and Benjamin, close to where the temple would later stand.
b: The other Levites are spread through the north and east. Traditional readers see God's foresight in placing the priests near the future temple. Many critical scholars take the pattern as a sign that the list was drawn up, or revised, after Jerusalem became the only sanctuary. Anathoth (21:18), home of the priest Abiathar and of Jeremiah, belongs to this group (1 Kings 2:26; Jeremiah 1:1).

a: The Gershonites
p: The three Levite clans named in Exodus 6 and given tasks in Numbers 3–4.
b: Kohath's clan carried the holiest things, Gershon the curtains and coverings, Merari the frames and posts of the tabernacle (Numbers 3:21–37; 4:1–33). Aaron's line was part of Kohath (Exodus 6:16–20). The lots here repeat that order of rank: Aaron's priests first, then the rest of Kohath, then Gershon, then Merari.

a: which are named here one by one
p: 1 Chronicles 6:54–81 gives the same list with a dozen differences in names.
b: Chronicles has Ashan for Ain (21:16), lacks Juttah and Gibeon, lacks Eltekeh and Gibbethon, has Jokmeam for Kibzaim, Aner and Bileam for Taanach and Gath-rimmon, Ashtaroth for Beeshterah, Kedesh for Kishion, Hukok for Helkath, Hammon for Hammoth-dor, Kiriathaim for Kartan, and Rimmono and Tabor for Zebulun's four towns. Some are spelling variants, some copying errors, some different towns. Most scholars think Chronicles drew on a form of this list; A. Graeme Auld argued the reverse.

a: But the fields of the town and its villages they had given to Caleb son of Jephunneh
p: Hebron was Caleb's inheritance (14:13–14) and also a priests' town. The verse explains how.
b: The priests lived in the town and used its common land; Caleb's family owned the fields and outlying villages. The same pattern held everywhere: Levites lived among the tribes without owning their farmland. Hebron was also a city of refuge (20:7) and later David's first capital (2 Samuel 2:1–4).

a: Taanach with its pastureland and Gath-rimmon with its pastureland
p: Gath-rimmon already appeared in Dan's list (21:24). Here it is probably a copying error for Ibleam.
b: 1 Chronicles 6:70 reads "Aner and Bileam" for Manasseh's two towns, and Bileam is Ibleam, a town of Manasseh (17:11). A scribe's eye likely slipped to the line above. The Greek has yet another name. Most commentators read Ibleam here.

a: forty-eight towns with their pasturelands
p: Scholars have dated the Levitical town list to Joshua's time, to David and Solomon, to Josiah, or after the exile.
b: Traditional readers take it as the list Joshua made as Numbers 35:7 required. W. F. Albright and Benjamin Mazar dated it to the united monarchy, when royal officials and Levites may have been placed in border towns (compare 1 Chronicles 26:30–32). Others place it under Josiah or later, or see it as an ideal map like Ezekiel 48. A. Graeme Auld argued that the list in Joshua grew out of the shorter list in 1 Chronicles 6, not the other way round, and so is late. Another argument for a later date is that some towns, such as Heshbon, show little sign of settlement in the Late Bronze Age. One argument for an early date is that some towns on the list were later lost to Israel.

a: So the LORD gave Israel the whole land he had sworn to give their ancestors
p: After chapters of unconquered towns, the narrator says every promise came true. How do these fit?
b: 13:1 said much land remained; 15:63, 16:10 and 17:12 tell of towns not taken; 23:4–5 speaks of nations left. Yet here the whole land is given. Traditional readers say the land was given in principle and the enemy's power broken, while full possession waited on Israel's faithfulness (23:12–13). Others see an ideal summary from the Deuteronomistic writer, set against older notes of failure. Hebrews draws its own conclusion: "If Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken afterward about another day" (Hebrews 4:8).

a: The LORD gave them rest all around
p: Deuteronomy promised rest in the land. Joshua says it came. Later books say it came again and was lost again.
b: Moses promised, "He will give you rest from all your enemies around you, and you will live in safety" (Deuteronomy 12:10). The same promise is said to be kept here, in 22:4 and 23:1, and again under David and Solomon (2 Samuel 7:1; 1 Kings 5:4). Psalm 95:11 and Hebrews 3–4 read God's rest as something still offered.
r: Deuteronomy 12:9–10; Deuteronomy 25:19; 22:4; 23:1; 2 Samuel 7:1; 1 Kings 5:4; Psalm 95:11; Hebrews 4:1–11

a: Not one of all the good words the LORD had spoken to the house of Israel fell short
p: The Hebrew says no word "fell." A promise that fails is pictured as dropping to the ground.
b: Of Samuel it is said that the LORD "did not let a single one of his words drop to the ground" (1 Samuel 3:19). Joshua repeats this line in 23:14, and Solomon echoes it at the temple's dedication: "Of all the good words he spoke by the hand of Moses his servant, not one word has fallen short" (1 Kings 8:56). The "good words" are God's promises of land, rest and blessing.

a: when I gave you orders, you listened to me every time
p: The eastern tribes had sworn to follow Joshua (1:16–18). He now praises them for keeping their word.
b: In Numbers 32 they promised to cross armed ahead of their brothers, and Moses warned, "be sure your sin will find you out" if they did not (Numbers 32:23). They kept faith through the whole war. The chapter opens with praise before it turns to a crisis, so the reader knows these tribes are loyal before the altar raises doubts.

a: Love the LORD your God and walk in all his ways
p: Joshua's charge is a string of Deuteronomy's favorite phrases.
b: Compare Deuteronomy 11:22, "to love the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways and to hold on to him," and Deuteronomy 10:12. Love, walking, keeping, holding on and serving "with all your heart" are the vocabulary of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:5). Scholars count this among the clearest marks of the Deuteronomistic writer in Joshua.

a: Share the plunder from your enemies with your brothers
p: Soldiers and those who stayed home share the spoil. David later made the same rule.
b: After the war with Midian, half the spoil went to the fighters and half to the community (Numbers 31:27). David ruled that those who guard the baggage get the same share as those who go into battle (1 Samuel 30:24–25). Here the eastern soldiers go home rich and are told to share with the families who stayed behind across the Jordan.

a: They came to Geliloth by the Jordan in the land of Canaan
p: The altar seems to stand on the west bank, "in the land of Canaan." Some read it as the east bank.
b: 22:10 says "in the land of Canaan," and 22:11 says "on the Israelites' side," both pointing to the west bank, on the way home. If so, the eastern tribes built a claim on the western side, which made the altar more alarming. Others read 22:11 as "opposite the land of Canaan," placing it on the east bank. "Geliloth" ("circles") may be the same as the Geliloth of 18:17 or another stone circle; no site has been firmly identified.

a: a big altar for all to see
t: An altar meant to be seen
p: Literally "an altar great in appearance." Its size was the point: it was a monument.
b: The tribes later explain that the altar was a copy, never meant for sacrifice (22:26–28). A large altar visible from far off would serve as a landmark and a reminder. The phrase prepares for its name and purpose in 22:34.

a: ready to go up and fight them
t: On the edge of civil war
p: Israel is ready to attack its own tribes over an altar. Deuteronomy commanded war against an Israelite town that turned to other gods.
b: Deuteronomy 13:12–18 orders the destruction of any Israelite town that leads people to serve other gods. A rival altar looked like the start of that (Deuteronomy 12:5–14). This time Israel sends a delegation first and listens, and war is avoided. In Judges 20 Israel does go to war against Benjamin, with Phinehas as priest (Judges 20:28). Readers have long held up Joshua 22 as a model of asking before attacking.

a: Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest
p: The priest who speared an Israelite and a Midianite woman at Peor now leads a peace mission.
b: At Peor Phinehas acted on the spot, and God gave him "a covenant of peace" (Numbers 25:7–13). He also went as priest in the war against Midian (Numbers 31:6). His presence warns the eastern tribes how seriously Israel takes this, yet here his zeal takes the form of words, questions and finally relief (22:30–31).

a: You have acted unfaithfully against the God of Israel!
p: Ma'al means "act unfaithfully" against what belongs to God. It is the word used of Achan (7:1).
b: Ma'al is treachery against God's holy things or his covenant (Leviticus 5:15; 26:40). Its use links this scene with Achan, who "acted unfaithfully" with the things under the ban (7:1; 22:20). In both cases the leaders fear that one group's act will bring God's anger on all Israel. Phinehas uses the word again in 22:31 when he finds there was no breach after all.

a: Is the guilt of Peor too small a thing for us?
p: At Peor Israel worshiped Baal and a plague killed thousands. The guilt, they say, still clings.
b: Numbers 25 tells how Israel joined the worship of Baal of Peor; "Those who died in the plague were twenty-four thousand" (Numbers 25:9). Numbers 31:16 blames Balaam's advice (see 13:22). Phinehas, who stopped the plague, now says Israel is still not clean of it. The sense is of shared guilt that lasts, like Hosea 9:10 and Psalm 106:28–31.

a: Is the land you hold unclean?
t: Is the land east of the Jordan less holy?
p: The western tribes suggest the eastern land might be "unclean," outside the land the LORD holds.
b: The promise in Numbers 34:12 made the Jordan the eastern border of Canaan; the land beyond was added at the eastern tribes' request (Numbers 32). So "the land the LORD holds" is where his tabernacle stands. Later Jewish law kept a distinction: the Mishnah records the view of Rabbi Yose the Galilean that firstfruits are not brought from beyond the Jordan, since it is not "a land flowing with milk and honey" (Mishnah Bikkurim 1:10). The generous offer here, to share western land, is the heart of the speech.

a: When he acted unfaithfully about the things under the ban
p: Achan's theft (chapter 7) cost Israel a defeat at Ai and many lives. One man's act can bring trouble on all.
b: See 7:1–26. The point here is corporate: "He was one man, but he did not perish alone in his guilt" (22:20). If one family's theft brought defeat, how much more a whole tribe's rival altar? The Bible holds both corporate and personal responsibility (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20), and this chapter leans on the first.

a: God of gods, the LORD! God of gods, the LORD!
p: El, Elohim, YHWH: three names of God, said twice, as a solemn oath.
b: El is the old word for God, Elohim the usual one, and YHWH his personal name ("the LORD"). Psalm 50:1 opens with the same three names. The Plain English follows the old rendering "God of gods" (compare Deuteronomy 10:17); many versions print "The Mighty One, God, the LORD." Saying the names twice is the strongest oath the tribes can make, calling on God himself as witness: "He knows."

a: It will be a witness between us and you
p: The altar is a memorial, like the stone heap of Jacob and Laban, and like Isaiah's future altar in Egypt.
b: Jacob and Laban built a stone heap and called it "heap of witness" (Genesis 31:44–52). Joshua later sets up a stone "witness" at Shechem (24:27). Isaiah 19:19–20 foresees "an altar to the LORD in the middle of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border. It will be a sign and a witness." In each case the object speaks for people who are not present, keeping a relationship in memory.

a: Look at this copy of the LORD's altar
p: Tavnit means "pattern, model." The tribes built a replica of the altar at the tabernacle, to show they shared in it.
b: Tavnit is the word for the "pattern" of the tabernacle shown to Moses (Exodus 25:9, 40). The tribes' defense rests on one sanctuary: sacrifice belongs only at the LORD's altar (Deuteronomy 12:5–14; Leviticus 17:8–9). Many critical scholars therefore read the story as written from a later point of view, when Jerusalem's temple was the only lawful altar. Traditional readers see the same law already in force at Shiloh. Either way, the story affirms that the tribes east of the Jordan belong to Israel.

a: This day has shown us that the LORD is among us
p: Phinehas, who came ready for war, ends by thanking God. Israel stays one people on both sides of the river.
b: "You have kept the Israelites safe from the LORD's hand" (22:31): by remaining faithful, the eastern tribes spared the whole nation from judgment. Jewish teachers have used the story as a lesson in judging others favorably and asking before accusing; Christian preachers have used it as a lesson in church unity. Pseudo-Philo's Biblical Antiquities (first century AD) retells the episode at length.

a: A long time later
p: Joshua says goodbye twice, in chapter 23 and again in chapter 24. Why two?
b: Chapter 23 is a speech to the leaders in the style of Deuteronomy, like Moses' last speeches and Samuel's (1 Samuel 12). Chapter 24 is a covenant ceremony with all the people at Shechem. Martin Noth thought chapter 23 was the Deuteronomistic writer's ending to the book, and chapter 24 an older tradition added later. Traditional readers take them as two events: a private charge, then a public covenant. Read together, the first warns and the second commits.

a: Be very strong, then
p: God told Joshua to be strong and keep the law (1:7–8). Now Joshua tells the people the same.
b: "Do not turn off to the right or to the left" goes back to Deuteronomy 5:32 and 28:14. The "book of the law of Moses" is the written Torah, which Joshua was told to keep in his mouth day and night (1:8). The charge given to the leader at the start of the book is handed to the whole nation at its end.

a: Do not even speak the names of their gods
p: The verb is "cause to remember," that is, to invoke a god by name in worship or oath.
b: Exodus 23:13 says, "Do not even mention the names of other gods; they must not be heard coming from your mouth." Calling on a god's name was how one prayed to it or swore by it. Psalm 16:4 has the faithful one say he will not take their names on his lips. The four verbs, invoke, swear, serve, bow down, move from words to worship.

a: hold on to the LORD your God
t: Holding on: to God or to the nations
p: Dabaq, "hold on to, cling," is used for God here and for the nations in 23:12. Israel must choose whom to hold.
b: Dabaq is the verb of marriage in Genesis 2:24 and of Ruth's clinging to Naomi (Ruth 1:14). Deuteronomy uses it for loyalty to God (Deuteronomy 10:20; 11:22). Joshua sets the two uses side by side: hold on to the LORD (23:8), or hold on to the remaining nations by marrying them (23:12). Loyalty is pictured as a marriage bond.

a: One of you makes a thousand run
p: A covenant blessing from Leviticus 26:8, and its reverse in the Song of Moses.
b: Leviticus 26:8 promises, "Five of you will chase a hundred, and a hundred of you will chase ten thousand." The Song of Moses turns it around for an unfaithful Israel: "How could one chase a thousand / and two make ten thousand run, / unless their Rock had sold them off" (Deuteronomy 32:30). Samson killed a thousand with a donkey's jawbone (Judges 15:15). The point is that victory comes from God, not numbers.

a: Suppose you marry them
p: Joshua forbids marrying the remaining Canaanites. The reason given is religious, not racial.
b: Deuteronomy 7:3–4 forbids marrying the peoples of the land "for they will turn your sons away from me." Ezra and Nehemiah later applied this harshly (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27). Yet the book of Joshua itself welcomes Rahab and her family (6:25), and Ruth the Moabite becomes David's ancestor. Jewish and Christian interpreters have generally read the ban as about worship (23:7, 16), and the warning came true in Judges 3:5–6. Readers who wrestle with the ethics of these texts note how easily such commands were later turned against outsiders.
r: Deuteronomy 7:3–4; Exodus 34:15–16; Judges 3:5–6; 1 Kings 11:1–8; Ezra 9:1–2; 6:25; Ruth 4:13–17

a: a lash on your sides and thorns in your eyes
p: Moses had warned that the nations left behind would become "thorns in your eyes." Judges shows it happening.
b: Numbers 33:55 says, "those you leave there will become barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides." Judges 2:3 has the angel of the LORD announce that the nations will be traps to Israel. Paul's "thorn in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7) may borrow the image. A trap and a snare are hunting gear: the danger is being caught without noticing.

a: today I am going the way of all the earth
p: A gentle way to say "I am about to die." David uses the same words to Solomon.
b: David says, "I am going the way of all the earth. So be strong. Be a man" (1 Kings 2:2). Death is the road everyone walks. Like Moses (Deuteronomy 31), Jacob (Genesis 49) and David (1 Kings 2), Joshua uses his last days to bind the next generation to God.

a: In just the same way the LORD will bring every bad word on you
p: God keeps his word both ways: the good word came true, and so will the warning.
b: The "bad word" means the curses of the covenant (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28), ending in loss of the land. The phrase "until he has wiped you out from this good land" sounds to many scholars like a voice from the exile, after 586 BC, explaining why it happened. Traditional readers hear a prophetic warning that Israel's later history proved true. Both agree the speech looks ahead to 2 Kings 17 and 25.

a: Suppose you break the covenant
p: "Break" is avar, "to cross over," the same verb used all through Joshua for crossing the Jordan.
b: Israel "crossed over" the Jordan into the land (chapters 3–4), and now Joshua warns them not to "cross over" the covenant, that is, overstep it. The covenant is a boundary like a river. In 7:11 the same phrase is used of Achan.

a: they came and stood before God
p: Shechem, between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, was Israel's oldest holy place in the land.
b: Abraham built his first altar in Canaan at Shechem (Genesis 12:6–7). Jacob bought land there and buried his household's foreign gods under the oak (Genesis 33:18–20; 35:4). The blessings and curses were read between its two mountains (Deuteronomy 27; 8:30–35). Later, Rehoboam went to Shechem to be made king (1 Kings 12:1), and the Samaritans worshiped on Gerizim (John 4:20). Excavations at Tell Balata found a massive temple fortress from the Bronze Age, which many link with the temple of El-berith, "God of the covenant" (Judges 9:46).
r: Genesis 12:6–7; Genesis 33:18–20; Genesis 35:1–4; Deuteronomy 27:1–13; 8:30–35; Judges 9:4; Judges 9:46; 1 Kings 12:1; John 4:20

a: The LORD, the God of Israel, says this
p: Many scholars see in chapter 24 the parts of an ancient treaty between a great king and a lesser one.
b: Hittite treaties of the 1300s BC typically open with the great king's name, review his past kindness, set out what the vassal must do, provide for a written copy, call witnesses, and list blessings and curses. Joshua 24 has the speaker named (24:2), a history of God's acts (24:2–13), the demand to serve him alone (24:14–15, 23), witnesses (24:22, 27), a written record (24:26) and a warning (24:19–20). George Mendenhall and Kenneth Kitchen saw this as evidence of an early date. Kitchen stressed that a long history of past kindness is typical of Late Bronze Age treaties and usually missing from the Assyrian treaties of later centuries. Dennis McCarthy argued that the chapter reports a covenant ceremony rather than reproducing a treaty, and that treaty language lasted for centuries. Lothar Perlitt and John Van Seters read the chapter as a late composition, from the age of Deuteronomy or after it.

a: and they served other gods
p: The Bible's only plain statement that Abraham's family worshiped other gods. Jewish tradition built stories on it.
b: Genesis says nothing of Terah's religion. Jewish tradition filled the gap: in a famous midrash, Abraham smashes the idols in his father's shop (Genesis Rabbah 38:13), and Jubilees 12 has him burn an idol house. The Passover Haggadah quotes this very verse: "In the beginning our ancestors served idols." Judith, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, has an early retelling too. There Achior the Ammonite says the family "did not want to follow the gods of their ancestors who were in the land of the Chaldeans" (Judith 5:7). They "worshiped the God of heaven" and were thrown out for it (Judith 5:8). Joshua's point is that Israel's story began with God's choice, not with a family already faithful.
r: Genesis 11:26–32; Genesis 12:1–3; Genesis 31:19; Genesis 35:2; Nehemiah 9:7; Judith 5:7–8

a: he set darkness between you and the Egyptians
p: Exodus 14:20 tells of the cloud and the darkness standing between the two camps.
b: "It came between Egypt's camp and Israel's camp. The cloud was there, and the darkness" (Exodus 14:20). The word here, ma'afel, appears nowhere else in the Bible. Notice how the speech moves between "your ancestors" and "you": the generation at Shechem is told it saw the sea with its own eyes. Every generation is to remember the exodus as its own story.

a: got up and fought against Israel
p: Numbers tells of no battle with Moab. Balak's "war" was his attempt to have Israel cursed.
b: Jephthah later asks of Balak, "Did he ever pick a quarrel with Israel? Did he ever make war on them?" (Judges 11:25), implying he did not. The verb here (lacham) can describe hostility of any kind, and Balak's weapon was Balaam's curse. God turned it to blessing (Numbers 22–24; Deuteronomy 23:4–5).

a: The men who held Jericho fought you
p: Chapter 6 shows Jericho shut up and its walls falling, with no battle. Here its "lords" fought Israel.
b: Ba'ale Yericho, "the lords (or citizens) of Jericho," may simply mean they resisted, shutting the gates and sending men after the spies (2:2–7). Some read a hint of a fuller war tradition behind chapter 6. The list of seven peoples is the standard list from Deuteronomy 7:1. On the archaeology of Jericho, see chapter 6.

a: I sent the hornet out in front of you
p: Exodus and Deuteronomy promised it. Is it a real insect, panic, or a symbol of Egypt?
b: Exodus 23:28 says, "I will send the hornet in front of you, and it will drive out the Hivites, the Canaanites and the Hittites from before you" (see also Deuteronomy 7:20). Readers have taken it as real swarms; as a figure for terror, like "my terror" in Exodus 23:27; or, following John Garstang, as Egypt, whose kings used the bee as a royal sign and whose raids weakened Canaan before Israel came. The word tsir'ah is rare and its exact meaning is not certain.

a: a land you had not worked on
p: Moses had said the same: towns they did not build, vineyards and olive trees they did not plant.
b: Deuteronomy 6:10–11 promised "large, fine cities that you did not build ... vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant," with a warning not to forget the LORD when full. Joshua's history ends on grace: "Your sword and your bow had no part in it" (24:12). Readers concerned with the ethics of conquest point out the other side: those vineyards had been someone else's. The text itself frames them as a gift that must be answered with loyalty.

a: wholeheartedly
p: Tamim means "whole." Said of animals, it is "flawless"; said of people serving God, "wholehearted" or "blameless."
b: The same word describes the flawless animals of the sacrifices (Leviticus 1:3) and people whose loyalty is undivided: Noah was "blameless in his generations" (Genesis 6:9), and God told Abram, "Go about your life in my sight, and be whole" (Genesis 17:1). Deuteronomy 18:13 asks Israel to be tamim with the LORD. Joshua asks for service with nothing held back, joined to emet, "faithfulness." Judges 9:16 uses the same pair of words for acting in good faith.

a: Get rid of the gods your ancestors served on the far side of the River and in Egypt
p: At this same place, Jacob once had his household give up their foreign gods.
b: "Jacob hid them under the oak that is by Shechem" (Genesis 35:4). Joshua's call to get rid of the gods, at Shechem, near an oak (24:26), repeats the scene. The mention of gods served "in Egypt" is striking; Ezekiel 20:7–8 and 23:3 also say Israel worshiped idols there. The demand implies that some still had them (24:23).

a: decide for yourselves today who it is you will serve
