p: Joshua puts the choice to the people, and makes his own: "I and my family will serve the LORD" (24:15).
b: The offer is real, but loaded: the only options besides the LORD are the gods their ancestors left or the gods of the land they just took. Moses had said, "Choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19), and Elijah would ask, "How long will you limp along on two crutches?" (1 Kings 18:21). Joshua's words about his household have become one of the best-known lines in the Bible, hung on the walls of Christian homes and quoted at Jewish and Christian weddings and covenant renewals.

a: You will not be able to serve the LORD
p: After the people promise loyalty, Joshua tells them they cannot keep it. Readers have puzzled over why.
b: Some read it as a test meant to draw a firmer promise, which it does (24:21, 24). Some read it as realism: the book of Judges proves him right. Christian readers since the Reformation have often heard Paul's point that the law shows people they cannot keep it (Romans 3:20; 7:7–25). Jewish readers stress the seriousness of covenant: a holy God cannot be served casually.

a: a jealous God
p: Jealous here means passionate and exclusive, as a husband is for his wife. It is not petty envy.
b: The Ten Words say, "I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God" (Exodus 20:5), and Exodus 34:14 adds, "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God." This form, qanno, appears only here and in Nahum 1:2. "He will not forgive" translates lo yissa, literally "he will not carry" or "lift": God will not lift away the rebellion of a people who chose him and then left him.

a: a rule and a ruling
p: "A rule and a ruling" (choq and mishpat) recalls Marah, where God first gave Israel law.
b: At Marah, "There he set for them a rule and a law, and there he tested them" (Exodus 15:25). Joshua does the same at Shechem, at the start of life in the land. Some scholars think the words he "wrote" (24:26) were a short covenant law for the tribes, now lost or folded into the Torah.

a: Joshua wrote these words in the book of God's law
p: The Talmud says Joshua wrote his own book and the last eight verses of the Torah.
b: Bava Batra 14b–15a credits Joshua with the book of Joshua and with Deuteronomy 34:5–12, which tell of Moses' death. It also notes that the closing verses of Joshua, about his own death, were added by Eleazar and Phinehas. This verse, where Joshua writes in "the book of God's law," was read as support. Most modern scholars read Joshua as part of the Deuteronomistic History, written much later from older sources.

a: beneath the oak at the LORD's sanctuary
t: The oak and the standing stone
p: Sacred trees and standing stones marked holy places. At Shechem archaeologists found a large standing stone by the temple.
b: Abraham's altar stood at "the great tree of Moreh" (Genesis 12:6), and Abimelech was made king "by the oak of the pillar at Shechem" (Judges 9:6). Deuteronomy condemned the stones and trees of Canaanite worship (Deuteronomy 12:3; 16:21–22), yet this stone is set up as a witness to the LORD. Ernst Sellin's German excavators at Tell Balata found a large limestone standing stone, broken and fallen, in front of the temple fortress in 1926. G. Ernest Wright's team set it upright again in 1962 and linked it with this verse. Not all archaeologists accept the link.

a: It will stand as a witness against us
p: Ancient treaties called on gods as witnesses. Israel's covenant calls the people themselves and a stone.
b: Hittite treaties listed gods, mountains, rivers and heaven and earth as witnesses. Moses called "the heavens and the earth to testify against you" (Deuteronomy 30:19). Joshua makes the people witnesses against themselves (24:22) and gives the stone ears: it "heard everything the LORD said" (24:27). A stone outlasts the people who stood there; it keeps the oath in view for their children.

a: the servant of the LORD
t: Servant of the LORD at last
p: Through the book Moses is "the servant of the LORD." Joshua receives the title only at his death.
b: Joshua began as "Moses' assistant" (1:1). The title "servant of the LORD" (eved YHWH) is used of Moses again and again in this book, and is given to Joshua only here and in Judges 2:8. His age, 110, matches Joseph's (Genesis 50:26) and was the ideal life span in Egyptian texts.

a: As long as Joshua was alive, Israel served the LORD
p: Faithfulness lasted as long as those who had seen God's work. Judges 2:7–10 tells what came next.
b: Judges 2:7–10 repeats this verse and then adds, "Then came a generation after them that knew nothing of the LORD, or of the work he had done for Israel" (Judges 2:10). The Greek text of Joshua places this verse before the report of Joshua's death, the same order Judges uses. Faith that rests on memory must be taught to the next generation (Deuteronomy 6:20–25).

a: Joseph's bones
p: Joseph's last wish is fulfilled. His bones, carried out of Egypt, are buried at Shechem.
b: Joseph had said, "When he does, carry my bones up from here" (Genesis 50:25), and Moses took them along (Exodus 13:19). Hebrews 11:22 counts this among acts of faith. The burial plot is the field Jacob bought (Genesis 33:19), which Jacob gave to Joseph (Genesis 48:22; John 4:5). Stephen's speech in Acts 7:16 combines this with Abraham's purchase at Hebron. A tomb at Nablus has been honored as Joseph's for many centuries. A "qesitah" was a unit of value whose weight is unknown.
r: Genesis 50:24–25; Exodus 13:19; Genesis 33:19; Genesis 48:22; Hebrews 11:22; Acts 7:15–16; John 4:5

a: Eleazar son of Aaron died
p: The book ends with three burials: Joshua, Joseph and Eleazar. The leaders of the conquest are laid to rest in the land.
b: Genesis ends with burials too, and with a promise of land (Genesis 50). Now the bones are in the land itself. Each man is buried in his own allotted ground: Joshua in his town, Joseph in his family's field, Eleazar on his son's hill. Samaritans and Jews have long honored tombs of Eleazar and Phinehas at Awarta, near Nablus. The Septuagint adds more lines after this verse (see the variant).
